query_text: where does the sound come from when you crack your knuckles

content.text:
The “crack” sound from cracking your knuckles mostly comes from **gas bubbles forming and collapsing inside the joint fluid**.

Your knuckle joints contain **synovial fluid**, a slippery liquid that helps the joint move smoothly. When you pull or bend a knuckle, you briefly **increase the space inside the joint**, which lowers the pressure in the fluid. Dissolved gases—mainly carbon dioxide—can rapidly come out of solution and form a bubble or cavity. That sudden change creates the popping/cracking sound.

This process is called **cavitation**.

A few related points:

- The sound is **not usually bones rubbing together**.
- You often can’t crack the same knuckle again immediately because it takes time for the gases to dissolve back into the fluid.
- Cracking knuckles has **not been clearly shown to cause arthritis**, though forceful or painful cracking may irritate tissues.

So, in short: the sound comes from a rapid pressure change in the joint fluid that creates a gas cavity/bubble.
